uncited: **Inputs:** A set of $N_\theta$ Radon projections $p(t, \theta_i)$ for angles $\theta_i$, where $i = 0, \dots, N_\theta-1$.
Each projection is a 1D signal of length $N_t$ (or $N_\rho$).
**Outputs:** A reconstructed 2D image $f(x, y)$ on a Cartesian grid of size $N_x \times N_y$.
**Projections:** Array `P[N_theta][N_rho]` storing the 1D Fourier transforms of the projections.
**Frequency Grid:** 2D array `F[N_x][N_y]` initialized to zero, representing the Cartesian frequency domain.
Coordinates $(U, V)$ map to array indices $(i, j)$.
For each projection angle $\theta_i$, compute the 1D Fourier transform of the projection $p(t, \theta_i)$ to obtain the slice $P(\nu, \theta_i)$ of the 2D Fourier transform of the object.
Iterate over all points $(\theta_i, \rho_k)$ in the polar frequency space derived from the projections.
Search for the nearest Cartesian pixel $(i, j)$ in the `F` grid surrounding $(U, V)$.
Interpolate the value $P(\rho_k, \theta_i)$ into `F[i][j]`.
Apply a 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to the reconstructed Cartesian frequency grid `F` to obtain the spatial domain image $f(x, y)$.
*   **Number of Projections ($N_\theta$):** Determines angular coverage.
*   **Grid Size ($N_x, N_y$):** Determines spatial resolution.
*   **Finite Angle Approximation:** The method is theoretically exact only for an infinite number of projections.
*   **High-Frequency Error:** Polar sampling density decreases as frequency increases (away from the origin).
*   **Uncovered Regions:** If the polar grid does not cover the entire Cartesian grid edges, high frequencies may be lost.
If the polar grid is scaled too large, regions may be unused.
*   **Resolution Dependence:** The irregularity of interpolation depends on the number of projections and image size.
**Time Complexity:** Reconstructing the Fourier space takes $N_\theta N_\rho = O(N)$ steps, where $N$ is the total number of samples.
**Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for the projections and the Cartesian frequency grid, proportional to $O(N)$.
**When to use:** Suitable for rotationally symmetric objects (via Hankel variant) or when frequency-domain processing is preferred.
The method was developed as an analytical alternative to iterative reconstruction techniques.
